examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
examples.problem: Calculate $\mathbf F(t)$ given that $\mathbf F'(t)= \left\langle \sec t \tan t, \,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf F(0)=\langle 0,\, 0\rangle.$
examples.worked_solution:
Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle \sec t \tan t,\,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $\mathbf F(0)=\left\langle 0,\, 0 \right\rangle$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0)=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡0+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨1+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $c_1=-1$ and $c_2=\dfrac 12.$ Consequently, 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\left\langle  \sec t - 1  , \,  -\dfrac 1 2\cos(2t)+ \dfrac12\right\rangle.
$$

feedback.problem:
Evaluate the following integral of a vector-valued function. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}⟨\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t},\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨$
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $⟩$
feedback.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}⟨\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t},\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t}\,\text{d}t,\,{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

For the first component, let $u=3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t$, so $\text{d}u={csc}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second component, we integrate directly:

$$
\int -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}⟨\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t},\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t){|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2},\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2),\,2\,(0-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨ln\,(\frac{3}{2}),\,-\sqrt{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨ln\,(\frac{3}{2}),\,-\sqrt{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$
